modules.checkpointPrompt: Explain why a 20-character passphrase like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is more secure than a short complex password like 'P@ss1!'. Consider entropy and cracking resistance in your answer.
checkpointCriteria: Must mention password length/entropy as the primary strength factor
Must acknowledge that short complex passwords can be brute-forced
Must reference that passphrases are easier to remember yet harder to crack
Should mention dictionary attacks or brute-force attacks

modules.title: Multi-Factor Authentication & Social Engineering
modules.subtitle: Phishing, Credential Theft & MFA Tokens
topics: Password reuse dangers across multiple accounts
keyFacts: Attackers can often send malicious emails designed to trick people into revealing their login credentials.
Compromised passwords may lead to stolen money or information.
Attackers could use your password to log into your account and impersonate you.
They might contact your friends, family, coworkers — even your organization's customers and vendors.
If you use the same password across multiple accounts, attackers only need to trick you once to gain access to all of those accounts.

modules.checkpointPrompt: You receive an email from 'IT-Support@groupernent-berkine.com' asking you to verify your credentials by clicking a link. Identify at least three red flags and describe what you should do.
checkpointCriteria: Must identify the typosquatted domain (groupernent vs groupement)
Must mention urgency/pressure tactics as a red flag
Must recommend not clicking the link
Should mention verifying through official channels

modules.title: Authentication Hygiene & Credential Storage
modules.subtitle: Phishing Triage & Secure Habits
topics: Creating long, unique passwords and PINs
keyFacts: Good cybersecurity habits can help you protect your accounts and your organization's systems.
Always create long, unique passwords and PINs.
Be cautious with any unexpected email that prompts you to log into a website, application, or system.
When it comes to passwords and PINs, make them strong, and keep them safe.
Don't let attackers make you their pawn in the cyber game.

modules.checkpointPrompt: A colleague asks to borrow your corporate login credentials 'just for a minute' to access a shared resource. What should you do and why? Also describe how you would securely store your own passwords.
checkpointCriteria: Must refuse to share credentials under any circumstances
Must mention the principle of individual accountability
Should recommend the colleague contact IT for proper access
Must mention using a password manager for credential storage
Should mention that shared credentials violate zero-trust principles

fullTranscript: Passwords and PINs are fundamental tools for keeping accounts and private information secure. Using strong, unique passwords is critical in your personal and professional life. Attackers can often guess simple, common passwords, or crack them with readily available software. Increasing complexity and length can strengthen passwords, making them more difficult to crack. Don't forget to keep passwords safe! Attackers can often send malicious emails designed to trick people into revealing their login credentials. Compromised passwords may lead to stolen money or information. Attackers could use your password to log into your account and impersonate you. They might contact your friends, family, coworkers — even your organization's customers and vendors. And if you use the same password across multiple accounts, attackers only need to trick you once to gain access to all of those accounts. Luckily, good cybersecurity habits can help you protect your accounts and your organization's systems. Always create long, unique passwords and PINs. And be cautious with any unexpected email that prompts you to log into a website, application, or system. When it comes to passwords and PINs, make them strong, and keep them safe. Don't let attackers make you their pawn in the cyber game.

indicators: Urgent or threatening language creating pressure
Requests for credentials or personal information
Generic greetings instead of personalized addressing
recommendedActions: Do not click any links or download attachments
Forward the original email to the security team
Contact the alleged sender through verified channels
